items.title: An 18-year-old's failed antimalarial attempt founded the synthetic dye industry
items.claim: In 1856 William Henry Perkin, an 18-year-old chemistry student in London, was trying to synthesise the antimalarial quinine from coal tar. He failed. The black sludge he produced, when washed with alcohol, gave a brilliant purple solution. He had made mauveine — the first synthetic dye.
items.prompt: Why did Perkin's mauve change the world?

options.text: It launched the synthetic organic dye industry, which became the seedbed of pharmaceutical chemistry, plastics, photography and modern industrial chemistry — particularly in Germany

items.reveal:
Perkin was working in his home laboratory during the Easter holiday. The bench was a board across the bathtub. He oxidised aniline (from coal tar) with potassium dichromate and got a tarry mess. Cleaning the flask with alcohol, he noticed an intense purple solution.

He filed a patent (despite being a minor), set up a factory at age 19 with his father and brother, and made a fortune. Queen Victoria wore mauve to her daughter's wedding in 1858. The colour exploded across European fashion.

Germany rapidly built on the industry. By 1900 BASF, Hoechst, Bayer and Agfa dominated synthetic chemistry and were turning out hundreds of new dyes. Aspirin (Bayer, 1899) and Salvarsan (Ehrlich, 1909) came out of the same dye-research tradition.

Perkin retired wealthy at 36 to do pure research.
items.why: An accidental failure can found an entire industry. The dye industry seeded pharmaceutical chemistry and modern materials science.

items.title: A buffer works best when pH = pKa — even though that means it's only half-effective
items.claim: A buffer is maximally effective at resisting pH change when [HA] = [A-], which means pH = pKa by Henderson-Hasselbalch. Counter-intuitively, this is when only half the acid is dissociated — not when you've added the most base.
items.prompt: Why does maximum buffering happen at half-neutralisation?

options.text: Because half-neutralisation is the only stable condition
Adding acid converts A- to HA and vice versa; the ratio [HA]/[A-] changes most slowly when the two are equal — small additions barely shift the log of the ratio, so pH barely changes
Buffers cannot work outside pH = pKa
Acid and base cancel only at pKa

items.reveal:
Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]).

If [HA] = [A-] (i.e. pH = pKa), then log term = 0 and small changes in [A-] or [HA] barely shift pH. Capacity is maximised within ±1 pH unit of pKa.

Move far from pKa and a buffer collapses: at pH = pKa + 2, [A-]/[HA] = 100; adding more acid takes it from 100 to 50 — only a 0.3 pH change at first, but the conjugate base is rapidly used up.

This is why biological buffers are tuned to the physiological pH they need to defend: phosphate (pKa2 = 7.2) inside cells, carbonate-bicarbonate (open system at pH 7.4) in blood. Choosing pKa to match the target pH is buffer design 101.
items.why: Maximum effectiveness coincides with 'only half the acid is reacted' — a useful surprise that follows directly from the log.

items.title: The same element you breathe shields the planet from UV
items.claim: Atmospheric oxygen is O2 — diatomic, vital for respiration. Ozone is O3 — pale blue, pungent, toxic at ground level and protective at altitude. Same element, two molecules, opposite roles.
items.prompt: Why does ozone behave so differently from O2?

options.text: O3's bent three-atom structure with delocalised pi bonding absorbs strongly in the 200-310 nm UV range; O2's MO structure has no comparable visible or near-UV absorption
O3 contains an extra proton per atom

items.reveal:
Ozone is bent with O-O-O angle about 117 degrees and two resonance structures. Its electronic transitions absorb the biologically damaging Hartley UV band.

The Montreal Protocol (1987) phased out CFCs to protect the stratospheric ozone layer. It is the most successful environmental treaty by measurable atmospheric impact. The ozone layer is now slowly recovering.

Ground-level ozone produced by photochemical smog damages lungs at parts-per-billion concentrations. Same molecule, life-saving at 30 km, lung-damaging at the surface.
items.why: Allotropes aren't just minor structural variants — they can be biologically and atmospherically opposite.
